title: What can one angle hide?
narration: Can one X-ray angle hide a narrowed artery? Look at this simulated angiogram. A nearby branch overlaps the area. When the view changes, the same narrowing is easier to see.
visual_direction: Open on the moving simulated contrast run, already filling the frame. During the first five seconds, rotate the same projected coronary tree until an overlapping branch clears the narrowing. Keep the lesion fixed in the three-dimensional model. Reveal the title after the question.

title: What the image shows
narration: A coronary angiogram is a moving X-ray study of the arteries that feed the heart muscle. Contrast enters through a catheter and outlines the channel that blood can pass through. The team watches the moving images to trace each artery and look for changes in the outline.
visual_direction: Follow the contrast front from a catheter tip at the coronary opening into an unbroken branching tree. Fade from warm anatomical art to monochrome imaging as contrast fills the same path. Keep the catheter tip at the opening, upstream of the lesion.

title: Follow the branches
narration: The team identifies the main branches before deciding where a narrowing is. In this example, the left main artery divides into the left anterior descending artery and the circumflex. A separate view shows the right coronary artery. Following the branches helps the team describe the exact location of a finding.
visual_direction: Use a frontal heart locator and an oblique simulated left-system projection. Trace the left main into LAD and circumflex, then move separately to the right coronary system. Keep the branch landmarks and the target location consistent. Show only the active artery label at a time.
on_screen_text: Left coronary system · Right coronary system

title: Spot the narrowing
narration: Here is one short narrowing. Contrast still passes through it and reaches the artery beyond. The team compares the narrowest part with a nearby reference segment and describes where the narrowing is, how long it is, and how severe it looks. A narrowing and a complete blockage look different on the images.
visual_direction: Move along the same LAD from a reference section to the short focal waist and then downstream. Match-cut to a vessel-wall cross-section showing plaque outside the contrast-filled channel. If showing an occlusion, use a separate visibly marked example and avoid claiming that every occlusion has no visible downstream vessel.

title: Why the team changes angle
narration: The X-ray turns three-dimensional arteries into a flat image. From one angle, branches can overlap or a segment can look shorter than it is. A second view can separate the branches and show more of the same narrowing. The clinician compares the recordings before describing what they see.
visual_direction: Return to the original LAD lesion and pivot the camera around the same tree. Freeze branch positions in the model, changing only camera projection. Show the same reference and target in both views so viewers can see overlap and apparent shortening without an artificial change in artery size.

title: Does it affect blood supply?
narration: The size of a narrowing on the picture gives the team one part of the answer. If its effect on blood supply is unclear, the team may use a thin pressure-sensing wire. Tests called F F R or I F R compare pressure beyond the narrowing with pressure upstream. The results help guide treatment decisions.
visual_direction: Keep the same stenosis. Transition from the contrast view to a schematic pressure wire crossing once, then show two clearly differentiated pressure locations. Avoid numerical cutoffs, drugs, pressure values and device settings. Leave room to show the separate physiology episode later.
on_screen_text: Picture and pressure answer different questions

title: When major arteries look open
narration: Sometimes the major arteries show no important blockage, even though a person has symptoms. Small blood vessels can work poorly, or a coronary artery can tighten temporarily. The care team uses the symptoms and other findings to decide whether more tests could help explain what is happening.
visual_direction: Use a distinctly labeled second illustrative case. Show an unobstructed major artery, then dissolve to conceptual microvessels and a separate transient spasm inset. Do not depict microvessels as visible on the ordinary angiogram or diagnose their condition from the main case.

title: How the findings guide care
narration: The result goes into a larger decision. The team considers the symptoms, urgency, which arteries are involved and any other tests. Care may include medicines and prevention, further assessment, a catheter procedure such as angioplasty and stenting, or a discussion about bypass surgery. In a heart attack, decisions may need to happen quickly.
visual_direction: Use a fully clothed, modest clinician and patient as optional simple silhouettes. Animate the case data into neutral choices one by one. Give every option equal visual weight. If showing acute urgency, introduce it as a separate context and use no timed instruction, percentage or treatment recommendation.

title: Three questions about the result
narration: When the team explains an angiogram, three questions can make the result easier to understand. Which artery was involved? Is there evidence that the narrowing affects blood supply? What follow-up or treatment does the team recommend? Those answers connect the picture to a plan for care.
visual_direction: Return to the main simulated angiogram. Reveal each question in a separate high-contrast beat with matching artery locator, physiology icon and follow-up mark. Keep one question visible at a time. End on the verified series color palette and retain the simulation disclosure.
on_screen_text: Which artery? · What effect? · What comes next?

title: Clinical sources
visual_direction: Hold a source and production card for eight seconds. Include the authentic Elysian logo, next episode title and room for YouTube end screens. Cite AHA, ACC/AHA/SCAI and ESC in the card and list full links in the description.
